title: Building the First Community
year: 1 AH — 622-623 CE, the first year in Madinah
teaser: He arrived with no land, no treasury, no army. Within a year Madinah had a masjid, a charter, and a name.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: Three peoples, one oasis, and no state
layers.content:
The Prophet ﷺ reached the town on a Friday — 12 Rabi'ul-Awwal of the first year of the Hijra, 27 September 622 CE. He had stopped first at Quba', on the edge of the oasis, and the reports of how long he stayed there do not agree: al-Bukhari preserves fourteen nights in one narration, some ten odd nights in another, and twenty-four nights in a third. He prayed his first Friday prayer in the valley of Banu Salim bin Awf with about a hundred men behind him. Then he took the lower floor of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari's house and lived there, while the city he had come to govern did not yet exist.

Yathrib was about to be renamed. Madinah is the short form of Madinat ar-Rasul, the City of the Messenger, and the new name arrived with him.

What he found was not a city but three peoples sharing one date-palm oasis. The Ansar — the Aws and the Khazraj — had been at each other's throats within living memory; the causes of their strife were deep-seated and the Bu'ath war recent enough that men on both sides remembered who had killed whom. The Emigrants were arriving homeless, jobless and often penniless, and their number grew week by week as permission to leave Makkah spread. A third group professed Islam without holding it; their head, Abdullah bin Ubai bin Salul, had been close to being made king over both Arab tribes before the Prophet ﷺ came and took that future from him. And around the settlement lived the Jewish tribes, long established, dominant in grain, dates, cloth and lending, watching.

Five hundred kilometres to the south sat Quraysh, who had seized the Emigrants' houses and property, and who would soon write to Madinah demanding that its guest be expelled or killed.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the narrations differing on the length of the stay at Quba', and the first Friday prayer
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The First Building
layers.subtitle: He carried the bricks with his own hands
layers.content:
The first task he took up was the masjid, and he set it on the ground where his camel had knelt. The land belonged to two orphans; it was bought from them. It held some graves of polytheists, and these were dug up and the ground levelled. Weeds, shrubs, palm trees and rubbish were cleared away, and trees were planted around it.

It was a plain building. Square, roughly a hundred yards to a side, walls of stone and adobe brick, a ceiling of palm leaves held up by two erected beams, three gates on each of the remaining sides. The qiblah was laid toward Jerusalem. Rooms for the Prophet's household were built beside it from the same stone and mud. Along the north side a space was set aside for Muslims who had neither family nor home in the town — men who slept in the mosque because there was nowhere else to sleep.

He carried the bricks and stones himself. While he worked he recited: 'O Allah, there is no bliss but that of the Hereafter; forgive the Emigrants and the Helpers.'

The call to prayer began in these same early months. The words of the adhan were shown to Abdullah bin Zaid in a dream, and the account is preserved by at-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, Ahmad and Ibn Khuzaymah.

The building was never only a place to pray. It was the school where Islam and its doctrines were taught. It was the assembly hall where the conflicting habits of the pre-Islamic years were argued out and reconciled. It was the headquarters from which the affairs of the Muslims were administered, and the room where the consultative and executive councils sat. A community with no palace and no treasury had one room, and everything happened inside it.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the building of the Prophet's Masjid; the adhan narrated by at-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, Ahmad and Ibn Khuzaymah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: Ninety Men in One Room
layers.subtitle: Brotherhood made a contract, not a feeling
layers.content:
With the masjid standing, he turned to the harder construction. Ninety men gathered in the house of Anas bin Malik — half of them Emigrants, half of them Helpers — and there the Prophet ﷺ gave the pairing of brothers his official blessing, one man to one man.

This was not a ceremony of sentiment. He attached a valid contract to it, touching blood and wealth rather than passing feeling. If one of the two paired men died, his property was inherited by his brother-in-faith. Brotherhood in faith was set above every distinction of race and kinship, on the principle that none is superior to another except by piety and fear of Allah. A Makkan refugee who owned nothing now held a legal claim on a Madinan household, and the Madinan held one on him.

What it produced is easier to measure than to describe. Sa'd bin ar-Rabi' of the Helpers said to his brother-in-faith Abdur-Rahman bin Awf: I am the richest man among the Helpers, and I am glad to share half my property with you; I have two wives, and I will divorce one so that you may marry her when her waiting period ends. Abdur-Rahman would take neither property nor home. He invoked blessings on him and asked one thing instead — direct me to the market, so that I may make my fortune with my own hands. He prospered, and married shortly after.

The Helpers then came to the Prophet ﷺ with a further offer: divide our orchards of palm trees equally between us and our brethren from Makkah. He was hesitant to lay that weight on them. It was settled instead that the Emigrants would work the orchards alongside the owners and the yield would be divided between them.

The Emigrants took only what let them make a reasonable living. Between the generosity on one side and the restraint on the other, a refugee crisis dissolved.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the brotherhood between the Emigrants and the Helpers, and the orchards of the Ansar
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: Two verses that settled two open questions
layers.content:
Two revelations reshaped what had just been built.

The inheritance clause inside the brotherhood was temporary. At about the time of the Battle of Badr the verse came down: «وأُولو الأَرحامِ بعضُهم أَولى ببعضٍ في كتابِ الله» — 'But those of blood relationship are nearer to one another in the decree of Allah.' (8:75) Inheritance returned to its ordinary course. The bond itself stayed; the legal mechanism that had carried the Emigrants through their destitute first year was withdrawn once they no longer needed carrying.

The qiblah of the new masjid had been laid toward Jerusalem. It did not stay there. «فَوَلِّ وَجهَكَ شَطرَ المَسجِدِ الحَرامِ» — 'So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram.' (2:144) The community that had just been given a home was turned to face the city that had expelled it. In the same passage it was told what it had become: «وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلناكم أُمَّةً وَسَطًا» — 'And thus We have made you a middle nation.' (2:143)

No revelation is recorded as having been sent down about the Charter or the treaty with the Jews themselves. Those documents were the Prophet's own governance, exercised with wisdom and intellect. What shaped them was what he taught daily in that mosque. Asked which merit in Islam is superior, he answered: 'That you provide food, and extend the greeting of peace to one whom you know and one whom you do not know.' He said: 'None of you believes truly until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.' And: 'The believers in their mutual love are like the human body — when the eye is in agony, the entire body feels the pain.'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Faith — on feeding and greeting, and loving for one's brother; Sahih Muslim — the believers as one body
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Document
layers.subtitle: A written constitution for a mixed city
layers.content:
The most durable thing built in that first year was written down.

The Charter of Islamic Alliance opened by declaring the Emigrants, the Helpers and those who followed and strove with them 'one nation to the exclusion of other people.' Each group would pay blood money from among itself and ransom its own prisoners honourably. No believer would be left poor for want of his redemption money or blood money. Whoever was rebellious or sought to spread enmity and sedition would have the hand of every God-fearing Muslim against him, even if he were his own son. No believer would kill a believer, nor support a disbeliever against one. The protection of Allah, the charter said, is one, and is extended equally to the humblest of the believers. Whichever of the Jews followed them would have aid and help, would not be injured, and would have no enemy aided against him. Whenever they differed over a matter, it was to be referred to Allah and to His Messenger ﷺ.

A separate treaty was concluded with the Jews of Madinah. Its first clause: the Jews of Bani Awf are one community with the believers; the Jews will profess their religion and the Muslims theirs. Each side would carry its own expenditure. If a third party attacked, each would come to the help of the other, and each would defend its own quarter of the town. Madinah was to remain sacred and inviolable to everyone who joined. There was no expulsion, no seizure of land or wealth.

Madinah and its suburbs then became a coalition state with the Prophet ﷺ at its head, and he went on entering similar treaties with the tribes living around it.

Carry this. He did not begin with an army. He began with a place to pray, a written agreement, and men made responsible for one another by name. Everything the next ten years demanded of that community rested on those three things, and not the other way round.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: When the Prophet's Masjid was first built in Madinah, which direction was its qiblah set toward?

options.text: The Ka'bah in Makkah
Jerusalem
Quba', where he had first stopped
Due east, toward the sunrise

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the building of the Prophet's Masjid
quiz.scholar_reflection: The mosque was built facing Jerusalem. The verse turning the qiblah toward al-Masjid al-Haram came afterwards (2:144), which means the first Muslims of Madinah prayed one direction, then obeyed a change.

quiz.prompt: How many men were paired as brothers in the house of Anas bin Malik?

options.text: Forty, all of them Emigrants
Ninety — half Emigrants, half Helpers
Three hundred and thirteen
Twelve, one from each clan of Madinah

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the brotherhood between the Muslims
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ninety men in one house, paired one to one. Not a speech about unity — a list of names, each with a matching name.

quiz.prompt: Sa'd bin ar-Rabi' offered his brother-in-faith Abdur-Rahman bin Awf half his property and one of his two wives. What did Abdur-Rahman ask for instead?

options.text: A share of the palm orchards
Directions to the market, so he could earn with his own hands
A house near the masjid
A camel and provisions to return to Makkah

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He refused property and refused a home. He prospered and married within a short time. The offer was real generosity; the refusal was real dignity. Both were praised.

quiz.prompt: How long did the Prophet ﷺ stay at Quba' before entering Madinah proper?

options.text: Exactly one night
Reports differ — al-Bukhari preserves fourteen nights, some ten odd nights, and twenty-four nights
A full lunar month, agreed by all narrations
He did not stop at Quba' at all

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited with the differing narrations in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sirah sources do not always agree, and honest reporting says so. What every narration agrees on is that he arrived at Quba' on a Monday and left on a Friday.

quiz.prompt: What ended the practice of brothers-in-faith inheriting from one another?

options.text: A decision of the consultative council in Madinah
The verse 'But those of blood relationship are nearer to one another in the decree of Allah' (8:75)
The Charter of Islamic Alliance
It was never practised — the brotherhood was symbolic only

quiz.scholar_reflection: The verse came down around the time of Badr and inheritance returned to its usual course. The measure lasted exactly as long as the need that produced it.

quiz.prompt: The brotherhood in Madinah was not a feeling but a contract touching property and inheritance. What do you make of binding generosity in law rather than leaving it to the heart?

options.text: Law protects the poor from depending on other people's moods
Obligation can hollow out generosity — what is compelled is not given
The contract existed because the need was extreme; ordinary times need less
The law set a floor, and the Ansar kept choosing to go far above it

quiz.slider_label: Leave it to the heart — Write it into law
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the brotherhood as a valid contract relating to blood and wealth
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar is careful on this point: it was a valid contract, not meaningless words or a passing impulse. And yet what the sources record are men exceeding it.

quiz.prompt: Abdur-Rahman bin Awf was offered half a man's wealth and asked for directions to the market instead. When you are the one in need, which instinct do you recognise in yourself?

options.text: Accept the help — refusing it can insult the giver
Take the smallest amount that gets me standing, then no more
Ask for work rather than wealth, as he did
I find it hard to ask at all, which is its own problem

quiz.slider_label: Accept what is offered — Ask for the market
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Note who is praised in this account: both of them. The one who offered half of everything, and the one who took none of it.

quiz.prompt: The masjid was built facing Jerusalem, then the community was turned to face Makkah — the city that had driven them out. What does being made to face what you fled do to a person?

options.text: It refuses to let grief become distance — the loss stays in view
It reframes Makkah as something to be returned to, not escaped
It shows obedience is not conditional on the direction feeling right
It made the community distinct from the peoples already in Madinah

quiz.slider_label: A wound reopened — A promise held in view
quiz.citation: Quran 2:144 — 'So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram'
quiz.scholar_reflection: Five times a day, for the rest of their lives, they faced the place that had tortured and expelled them. Eight years later they walked back into it.

quiz.prompt: The treaty with the Jews of Madinah guaranteed their religion, their wealth and their safety — concluded with neighbours whom the sources describe as already resentful of his arrival. How do you read that decision?

options.text: Justice is owed regardless of what the other side privately feels
It was strategy — he could not fight Quraysh and his own city at once
Written terms make later betrayal legible instead of arguable
He was offering them a real partnership, and meant it

quiz.slider_label: Guard against them first — Extend to them first
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — A Treaty With the Jews
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar states it plainly: he had no intention of following severe policies of expulsion, seizure of wealth and land, or hostility. The clauses gave full freedom in faith and wealth.

quiz.prompt: In his first year of actual power he built a mosque, paired ninety men, and wrote two treaties. No army was raised. What does that ordering tell you?

options.text: Internal cohesion has to exist before external strength means anything
He was buying time — Madinah could not have survived a fight that year
The mosque was the government, so building it was building the state
Whatever a community is for, that is what it should build first

quiz.slider_label: Secure the borders — Bind the people
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — A New Society Being Built
quiz.scholar_reflection: Badr came in the second year. By then Madinah had one identity, one law of dispute, and a treasury of obligations between men. The battle was possible because the year before it was spent this way.
